articles.title: RoboDoctor: Training-Free Recursive Self-Improvement for Robot Policies
articles.summary: Generalist robot policies and language-model agents provide complementary capabilities, but completing a task also requires adapting their use to the consequences of physical interaction. We study execution as a locus of adaptation: feedback guides the current action and supplies evidence for revising subsequent decisions under fixed model weights. We introduce RoboDoctor, a training-free framework that connects diagnosis, grounded action, and persistent experience across three revision targets. The harness allocates control between policy and agent; intervention determines when to assist while preserving useful policy behavior; and operation refines physical methods through observed effects. Linked experience records retain the reason for a decision, the attempted method, its outcome, and conditions for reuse. articles.title: I got tired of typing "do 1 and 3, skip 2" to Claude Code, so I built an approve/reject board
articles.summary: You ask Claude Code for ten improvements to your project. It answers with a tidy numbered list. Then the real work starts: you scroll, you type "do 1 and 3, skip 2 because we tried that, maybe 5 later," and you hope the agent maps your sentence back to the right items. Next week, in a new session, it proposes number 2 again. So I built ar-board, a Claude Code plugin that turns the list into cards on a local page. You judge each card with one key (approve, reject, or maybe) and a short reason. The agent gets back an exact list of what you approved, and your reasons go into a preferences file it reads before it proposes anything next time. One Python file, standard library only, MIT licensed. The panel opens in English, and an EN/PT toggle in its header switches it to Portuguese. The cards are in whatever language you and the agent are using. You can try a sketch of the board in your browser before installing. articles.title: A pre-flight checklist before domain continued pre-training
articles.summary: Your team picked an open weight checkpoint and a corpus. The tempting move is to schedule GPUs and iterate on the mix later. Joel Hron at Thomson Reuters and Fergal Reid at Intercom both describe training as staged pipelines where evaluation sits beside the data, and Hron treats retained capabilities as an explicit objective. I'd treat the run as blocked until you can answer the questions below. What training stage are you actually running? Most product teams are not pretraining from scratch. They adapt a base model in layers. Continued pre-training adds more unlabeled domain text on top of an existing checkpoint. Supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization teach labeled behavior. Agentic reinforcement learning teaches tool use inside a harness. articles.title: OpenAI Moderation API and GPT-4o-mini Chat Completions: JSON Schema Text Triage
articles.summary: Short answer: treat text moderation as a queue contract, not a prompt trick. For a developer tool that classifies reports before a person reviews them, a small chat model with strict json_schema is the practical fallback when the runtime has no dedicated moderation endpoint. Keep the result narrow: { "is_safe": boolean, "reason": string }. Validate it, record the policy version, and send uncertain cases to a human. The main trade is governance. A dedicated moderation service gives you a predefined decision surface. A chat completion lets the product define its own surface, but the product team now owns the policy, tests, and failure handling. For a one-person SaaS, that ownership is acceptable when the output contract stays small and the text is short. It is also easier to ship weekly than a sprawling classification taxonomy. articles.title: Claude Code hooks for teams: four hooks worth committing to your repo
articles.summary: Most teams start shaping Claude Code with instructions: a CLAUDE.md file that says "run the formatter," "never edit the lockfile," "use our logger." That works most of the time. But an instruction is something the model chooses to follow. On a long session, or a busy day, it sometimes doesn't. Hooks close that gap. A hook is a shell command that Claude Code runs automatically at a fixed point, such as after every file edit or before every command. It runs every time, whether or not the model remembers the rule. For a team, that changes what you can promise. "The agent should format its code" becomes "the agent's code is always formatted." Where team hooks live Hooks go in the same settings files as permissions. For a team, the one that matters is .claude/settings.json in the repository, committed like any other config. articles.title: 7 Mac Apps for Developers Who Run Claude Code, Codex and Cursor at the Same Time (2026)
articles.summary: Running one AI coding agent is easy. Running three at once (Claude Code refactoring in one terminal, Codex writing tests in another, Cursor open on the frontend) is where a Mac setup starts to creak. Windows pile up, the fans spin, diffs land faster than you can read them, and you find out you've hit a usage limit only when an agent stops mid-task. These are the seven apps I'd put on a Mac that runs agents in parallel. Most are free. 1. Ghostty: a fast terminal with native splits Free and open source: ghostty.org Agents that stream a lot of output need a terminal that renders quickly and doesn't slow down after an hour.
